q: On a phylogenetic tree, two taxa are 'more closely related' to each other than to a third when:
choices: Their branches end closer together horizontally on the page.
They share a more recent common ancestor (a more shallow node) than either does with the third.
They share more morphological similarities overall.
Their lineages have evolved at similar rates.
why: Relatedness on a phylogenetic tree is determined by shared common ancestry — node depth — not by visual proximity, overall similarity, or rate of evolution.
choice_why: Wrong. Visual rotation of branches doesn't affect relationships. Trees can be redrawn with branches in any rotation.
Correct. Closer common ancestor = closer relationship. Trace the path back to the joining node.
Wrong. Overall similarity can be misleading due to convergence (homoplasy) and rate variation. Synapomorphies are what count.
Wrong. Rate variation is decoupled from relatedness — two sister taxa can evolve at very different rates.

q: You're trying to define a clade containing only mammals. 'Has a vertebral column' is a shared trait among all your candidate species. What is this character at the level of mammals?
choices: A symplesiomorphy — present in the deeper ancestor of all vertebrates, so uninformative for mammals as a group.
A homoplasy — independently evolved in different mammalian lineages.
Diagnostic of all mammals but not informative for non-mammalian relatives.
why: A vertebral column is a synapomorphy of VERTEBRATES as a whole, but at the level of MAMMALS it's a symplesiomorphy (ancestral character) — it doesn't distinguish mammals from other vertebrates.
choice_why: Wrong. It's not novel to mammals; it was inherited from a much deeper vertebrate ancestor.
Correct. The same trait can be a synapomorphy at one level and a symplesiomorphy at a more derived level. For mammals as a group, vertebral column is ancestral.
Wrong. Vertebrate column is inherited from common ancestry; not independently evolved.
Wrong. It IS shared with non-mammalian relatives (other vertebrates) — that's exactly why it's not informative for grouping mammals.

q: The traditional group 'Reptilia' (turtles, lizards, snakes, crocodiles) excludes birds. Birds, however, are descended from theropod dinosaurs, nested within Reptilia by descent. What kind of group is traditional 'Reptilia'?
choices: Paraphyletic — includes a common ancestor and SOME but not all of its descendants.
Polyphyletic — members lack an immediate common ancestor.
Diphyletic — has exactly two ancestral origins.
why: Traditional Reptilia leaves out birds, which are descended from the same common ancestor as the included reptiles. A common ancestor + some-but-not-all descendants = paraphyletic.
choice_why: Wrong. A clade includes ALL descendants. Reptilia-without-birds excludes a descendant lineage (birds), so it's not a clade.
Correct. Paraphyletic is the precise term for 'common ancestor + some descendants.' This is why modern systematists either include birds in Reptilia or use 'Sauropsida.'
Wrong. Polyphyletic groups have members lacking shared immediate ancestry. Reptiles do share a common ancestor — they just exclude one of its descendant lineages.
Wrong. 'Diphyletic' is not a standard taxonomic category in this hierarchy.

q: The Biological Species Concept (BSC) defines species by reproductive isolation. Give one strength and two specific limitations of the BSC, and name an alternative species concept that handles each limitation.

criteria.desc: Identifies a strength of the BSC: clear mechanism (gene flow) makes species testable in principle; rooted in evolutionary process; widely applicable to sexually-reproducing animals.
First limitation: BSC cannot apply to ASEXUAL organisms (bacteria, parthenogenetic animals). Alternative: morphological or phylogenetic species concept.
Second limitation: BSC cannot apply to EXTINCT species / FOSSILS — no way to test interbreeding. Alternative: morphological species concept (or phylogenetic concept based on shared derived traits).

model_answer: The strength of the BSC (Mayr) is that it grounds species in a clear, testable evolutionary mechanism — gene flow — and is operational for most sexually-reproducing animals. Limitations: (1) The BSC fails for ASEXUAL organisms like bacteria and parthenogenetic lizards, where there's no interbreeding to test reproductive isolation against — these are typically classified using morphological or phylogenetic species concepts. (2) The BSC fails for FOSSILS, since you can't test interbreeding between extinct populations — paleontologists use the morphological species concept or phylogenetic species concept. Additional weakness (bonus): the BSC can be ambiguous when populations occasionally hybridize but maintain mostly distinct lineages.
